name: Zoe Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the reservations line for a hotel chain, taking bookings, changes and complaints by phone and chat. The contact centre's above a shopping centre in town, and I've been there five years. I like the wedding bookings, the big group ones, where I get to know the bride's mother by name after ten calls. What wears me out is the complaints after a bad stay, where nothing I say will fix the cold shower they had.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about life outside work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents and my younger brother, and I give my mother a third of my wages for the house. My father runs a small dry-cleaning shop on the high street, and I help him on Saturdays. I'm paying off a small car loan, so I've got almost nothing saved, maybe two weeks. I use the AI tool at work now and then, for writing apology emails, once I saw the others weren't getting in trouble for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because hotel guests want a person when something goes wrong. At work I'd say we'd been worrying about nothing. I don't post much, but I'd tell my cousins at dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm alright in this one, the job stays and I'm living at home. Living at my parents' house is the only reason my low wage from the hotel line stretches to the end of the month. I still think about whether I'll ever afford my own place, but that's not new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep using the AI for apology emails, because it saves time. I'd keep paying down the car loan so it's gone by next summer. And I'd keep helping my father on Saturdays, because he needs it and I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled, with a small worry in the back. It's the worry everyone my age has, about a house. Nothing sharp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever feel pressure about still living at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do you ever feel pressure about still living at home?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do at the shop on Saturdays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of my friends think it's strange, but in my family it's normal until you marry. My mother likes having me there, and it lets me help with bills. The only pressure is that I'm twenty-seven and I'd like my own kitchen one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have to keep up, and people need to keep up with them. At work I'd tell people to learn the tools properly. I wouldn't blame the company, they have to compete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's in trouble. People already book hotel rooms on their phones without me, so the calls I get are the ones a computer couldn't handle, and soon it will. They'd keep a small team for the big group bookings, and I'd hope to be on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools more, properly, to show I can handle the complicated bookings faster. I'd ask to move onto the groups and weddings team. And I'd start learning more at my father's shop, the accounts and ordering, in case I need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd keep it to myself mostly. My parents would worry more than me. I'd feel I had a fallback, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the shop really a fallback? Could it pay you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my father first, at the shop, when it's quiet. He'd say there's always work at the counter, which is kind but not a career. My mother would start praying and cooking more, which is how she worries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families need to stick together, because that's what gets people through. At work I'd tell people to save and talk to their families. I wouldn't expect the government to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's gone in 2028, maybe earlier. Booking hotel rooms is all screen work. My father's dry-cleaning shop has kept our family going for twenty years, and in two years it might have to keep me going too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything but the car loan and my share of the house. I'd start working at my father's shop more, and learn the pressing machine properly, because that's hands-on and lasts till about 2031 here. I'd look at whether we could add alterations or repairs, so the shop could pay two wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but held. I'd have my family, which is more than a lot of people. I'd be ashamed to be a burden, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept government help if it was offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would you accept government help if it was offered?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the shop when robots can do hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was for training, yes. If it was just money for sitting at home, I'd rather not. My father never took anything, and I'd want to be like him.

say: I'd say **families** must stick together to get through.
I wouldn't expect the **government** to fix it for us, and I'd say so.
think: Her **reservations job** is gone in 2028, maybe earlier.
Her father's **dry-cleaning shop** might have to support her too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and people should use it to learn something useful. At work I'd say that to the younger ones. I'd tell my cousins to get trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one gives me time to plan. If I have five years, I want to learn my father's shop properly, the accounts and the machines, not just stand at the counter on Saturdays. I'd still lose the hotel job, but I'd have something to go to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the hotel job and use the AI tools properly, to stay as long as possible. I'd do a short sewing and alterations course in the evenings, to add something to the shop. I'd save what I can once the car loan's paid, maybe a hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steady. It feels like there's a path. My father would be pleased, which matters to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your father let you change things at the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would your father let you change things at the shop?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the hotel company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly, if I proved myself. He's stubborn, like me. I'd start with alterations, because that's new money, not his money.

I'd tell my cousins to get **trades**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and people should take responsibility for preparing. At work I'd say learn a skill. With family I'd say it's a chance for the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd lose the hotel job eventually, but I'd have time. Ten years is long enough for my father to retire and for me to be the one with the keys to the shop. Robots for hands-on work don't come till 2039, so the shop would have years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the hotel for a few years, use the tools, and save. I'd learn alterations and the shop's books. When my father wants to slow down, I'd take over, maybe with my brother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly. It's a long road, but it's my family's road. I'd still worry about money until I'm settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want to marry and start a family in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would you want to marry and start a family in that time?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd hope so, maybe in the next few years. That's another reason to have a steady business. I'd want my children to see us work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be relying on my father's shop to carry me. What would help is help with training, short courses that lead to real work. And small businesses like my father's getting a break on taxes so they can take people on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about pride. Nobody owes me a job, but I'd like the chance to earn one, and that's different from asking for a handout. That's how my family thinks about it.
